paras: The Chanute Evergreen Park mass meeting was a night gathering of about 300 white residents of the Evergreen park second addition in Chanute, Kansas, on 12 August 1903, held at the partly built house of a Black woman, Mrs. Foster. The crowd, some of its members carrying clubs, resolved to press her to stop building and to tear the house down if she refused. The Topeka State Journal reprinted the Chanute Tribune's account under the headline "NEAR TO RACE WAR."

According to the Tribune, no Black residents yet lived in that part of Chanute's Fourth ward, and the residents of the new addition feared that if one "colored family" were allowed to build, others would follow. A real estate firm had already sold a second lot to a Black buyer who, the crowd's leaders understood, meant to build at once.

The residents met "three hundred strong" around the house's partly completed foundation and debated how to keep Black families out of the addition. Many favored buying the Black owners' lots by popular subscription, while others argued that this would set a bad precedent and give no protection against later arrivals. The meeting finally agreed to send a committee to Mrs. Foster to dissuade her from building, and, if it failed, to assemble again and "tear down the negro dwelling." The crowd, described as "three hundred laborers," dispersed near midnight.
No report of the committee's visit, of the house being finished or torn down, or of any official response appears in the coverage.

The episode is known from a single item, a Chanute dispatch in the Topeka State Journal of 13 August that quoted the local Tribune. The Tribune's text took the residents' point of view, calling the Foster family's arrival a "prospective invasion" of the addition's "quiet precinct," yet it also referred to the gathering as a "mob" and a "posse" inclined to violence. The Topeka headline and deck, "Crowd of 300 Whites Carrying Clubs," framed the meeting as a near riot, and the story closed by saying the club-carrying crowd "looked singularly sinister" as it left.

The single account is inconsistent about whether the crowd was armed: one garbled sentence calls those assembled "unarmed" and "for the most part peaceably inclined," while the headline and closing line say some carried heavy clubs.

reader.title: Chanute Evergreen Park mass meeting against a Black homebuilder
bases: A crowd of about 300 white residents met at a Black woman's partly built house and resolved to make her stop building, threatening to tear the dwelling down if she refused; no violence is reported (A1).
The only report is a Topeka State Journal reprint of the Chanute Tribune (A1); Black-press Chanute columns that week do not mention it (A2, A3).

accounts.label: Chanute Tribune (reprinted by the Topeka State Journal)
accounts.gist: Some 300 residents met at the partly built negro home to keep colored families out of the addition, agreed to send a committee to dissuade Mrs. Foster, and to tear the house down if she refused; the crowd dispersed near midnight.

framing.detail: The Tribune text adopts the residents' view ('prospective invasion of a negro family into the quiet precinct') while the Topeka headline 'NEAR TO RACE WAR' and the closing line that the club-carrying crowd 'looked singularly sinister' present it as a menace.

versions.value: Those assembled were 'unarmed' and 'for the most part peaceably inclined'
Some carried 'heavy clubs' (also in the headline deck), and the 'posse seemed inclined to resort to violence if necessary'

conflicts.note: Both versions are in the same article; the sentence calling the crowd unarmed is garbled ('unarmed except for the most part peaceably inclined').

sources.note: 'NEAR TO RACE WAR', Chanute dispatch reprinting the Chanute Tribune: 300 residents met at Mrs. Foster's partly built house, resolved to dissuade her or tear it down; the only report found.
quotes: They met three hundred strong around the partially completed foundation of the negro home and discussed the question of allowing a colored family to settle in the new addition.
It was finally agreed to appoint a committee to visit Mrs. Foster, the colored lady building the house, and attempt to dissuade her from building..
If the committee was not successful in its efforts then the residents would assemble and tear down the negro dwelling.
The posse seemed inclined to resort to violence if necessary to prevent such an occurrence.
the mixed crowd of three hundred laborers, some carrying heavy clubs, looked singularly sinister as it dispersed.
